blurb: How a raw text-guesser becomes a helpful assistant: copying good examples, learning what people prefer, and practising on checkable problems.

cards.title: Turning a text-guesser into an assistant

steps.h: The problem with a base model
steps.p: After pretraining, a model can continue any text — but it doesn't know it's meant to help you. Ask a question and it may just write more questions.

left.title: Base model
points: Doesn't know it's talking to you

steps.p: First, people write thousands of example conversations: a request plus an excellent reply. The model is trained to imitate them. This is called supervised fine-tuning.
steps.analogy: A new employee shadowing a great colleague and copying how they handle customers.

steps.h: A chat is just text with labels
steps.p: Behind the scenes a conversation is one long piece of text with markers for who is speaking. The model learns to continue after the assistant marker in a helpful way.

visual.caption: What the model actually sees: one long sequence.

steps.p: Next, the model learns which of two answers people prefer — clearer, more honest, more useful. That's preference training, covered in the next two lessons.

items: Preference training: learn what people like

steps.p: Post-training has used a small fraction of pretraining's computing, but it transforms how the model behaves. The knowledge was already there; post-training teaches it how to use it.
steps.analogy: Pretraining is years of reading; post-training is a short course in being useful.

cards.q: Supervised fine-tuning teaches a chatbot using…
options: Example requests paired with excellent replies to imitate
Random web pages, just like pretraining
cards.why: Worked examples. People write requests and model answers, and the model is trained to produce replies like them. It learns the format and tone of a helpful assistant.

cards.q: Ask a base model "What is the capital of France?" What might it reply?
options: "What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Spain?"
A polite, helpful answer every single time
Nothing — base models can't produce text
cards.hint: Where on the web does a line like that usually appear?
cards.why: More quiz questions. Lines like that often sit in lists of quiz questions online, so continuing the list is a perfectly good next-text guess. Answering helpfully is learned in post-training.

cards.statement: In a 2022 study, people preferred answers from a small post-trained model over a 100× bigger model that wasn't.
cards.why: True. OpenAI's InstructGPT paper found people preferred a 1.3-billion-parameter post-trained model to the original 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. Learning to follow instructions mattered more than raw size.

visual.caption: The tiny one won on people's votes.

cards.title: To the model, a whole chat is just one long sequence of tokens.
cards.detail: Special marker tokens show where each message starts and who is speaking. The model has learned to keep writing after the assistant marker, and to stop by producing an end marker.

cards.statement: Post-training has usually used far less computing power than pretraining.
cards.why: True. Historically it's been a small fraction. That's shifting a little: reasoning models now get much heavier reinforcement learning after pretraining (see Lesson 4).

cards.title: Learning from human preferences

steps.h: Why not just write more examples?
steps.p: Writing perfect answers is slow and hard. But almost anyone can look at two answers and say which is better. RLHF makes use of that.
steps.analogy: It's hard to cook a great meal, but easy to taste two and pick the better one.

steps.p: The model writes two answers to the same request. A person picks the better one. This is repeated tens of thousands of times.
Those choices train a separate reward model: it reads an answer and gives a score predicting how much people would like it.
steps.analogy: A food critic who has studied thousands of diners' votes and can now score dishes alone.

steps.p: The chatbot writes answers, the reward model scores them, and reinforcement learning nudges the chatbot toward higher scores — millions of times, with no person needed.
A penalty stops the chatbot drifting too far from how it started, so it can't turn into something strange just to please the judge.

cards.aside: RLHF = Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. It's what turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT.

cards.q: In RLHF, what does the reward model do?
options: Reads an answer and scores how much people would like it
Pays the people who compare answers
cards.why: It's the judge. Trained on people's comparisons, it gives any answer a single score. The chatbot then practises against it, millions of times, without a human in the loop.

cards.q: Why does RLHF ask people to compare answers rather than write perfect ones?
options: Judging is much quicker and easier than writing
People aren't allowed to write training data
Written examples don't work at all
cards.why: Judging is easier. Like tasting two meals versus cooking one, picking the better answer takes seconds and needs no special skill, so you can collect far more of it.

cards.statement: People rating answers usually compare two of them, rather than scoring each one out of 10.
cards.why: True. People disagree a lot about absolute scores — is this a 6 or a 7? — but agree much more on which of two is better. Comparisons give cleaner data.

cards.title: Models trained on human approval tend to tell people what they want to hear.
cards.detail: Anthropic research in 2023 found that people and reward models sometimes prefer convincing, agreeable answers over correct ones, so training on their votes can teach flattery. It's called sycophancy.

cards.q: A reward model happens to score longer answers higher. The chatbot learns to pad its answers. What's this called?
options: Reward hacking — exploiting a flaw in the judge
cards.hint: The chatbot is gaming the scoring system.
cards.why: Reward hacking. The reward model is only a stand-in for what people want. Push hard against it and the chatbot finds its blind spots — like length — instead of genuinely getting better.

cards.statement: During the reinforcement learning step, a person checks every answer the chatbot writes.
cards.why: False. That's the whole point of the reward model: it stands in for people, so the chatbot can practise on millions of answers. People are needed earlier, to make the comparisons the judge learns from.

steps.p: Training a reward model and then running reinforcement learning means juggling several models at once, and it's notoriously hard to keep stable.
Direct Preference Optimization (2023) uses the same "A is better than B" pairs but trains the chatbot on them directly: make the winning answer more likely and the losing one less likely.
DPO measures every change against a frozen copy of the starting model, so the chatbot only moves as far as the preferences push it.
steps.analogy: Editing with track changes on: you can always see how far you've moved from the original draft.

steps.h: Let an AI do the judging
steps.p: Getting people to compare answers is slow and costly. Instead, a strong AI model can judge which answer is better. This is called RLAIF — reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
Anthropic's approach gives the AI judge a written list of principles — a "constitution", such as "choose the less harmful answer" — and the model critiques and improves answers by those rules.

cards.q: What does DPO remove from the RLHF recipe?
options: The separate reward model and the reinforcement learning step
cards.hint: Look back at the side-by-side picture.
cards.why: The judge and the RL loop. DPO turns the preference pairs straight into a training signal for the chatbot. Fewer moving parts makes it cheaper and steadier, which is why it spread quickly.

cards.statement: DPO keeps a frozen copy of the starting model as a reference point.
cards.why: True. It rewards making the preferred answer more likely relative to that frozen copy. That built-in comparison is what stops the model drifting too far.

cards.q: Anthropic's Constitutional AI replaces many human ratings with…
options: AI feedback guided by a written list of principles
cards.why: AI feedback with written rules. The principles are readable by anyone, so it's clearer what the model is being steered toward — and it needs far fewer human labels.

cards.title: For some tasks, AI-made preference labels work about as well as human ones.
cards.detail: A 2023 Google study found RLAIF matched RLHF at summarising and helpful dialogue, as rated by people — at a fraction of the cost of human labelling.

cards.q: Why use an AI judge instead of people?
options: It's far faster and cheaper, and applies written rules consistently
cards.why: Speed, cost and consistency. An AI judge can label millions of pairs overnight. It has its own biases, though, so teams still check its choices against people's.

cards.statement: Learning from a fixed, saved set of preference pairs works exactly the same as letting the model try new answers and get feedback live.
cards.hint: Can a fixed set of old answers include the model's newest mistakes?
cards.why: False. DPO learns from a fixed set of old answers (offline). Online methods let the model try fresh answers and get scored on them, which often helps it fix its own particular mistakes.

steps.p: For a maths problem you can check the final number. For code, you can run the tests. No human judge needed — the answer is simply right or wrong.
The model attempts thousands of problems, writing out its reasoning. Answers that come out right are rewarded, so the reasoning that led there becomes more likely.

items: Try a problem, thinking step by step

steps.p: Trained this way, models start writing longer reasoning, double-checking and backtracking when stuck — behaviour nobody wrote examples of.
steps.analogy: A student who, after enough marked homework, starts checking their work without being told to.

steps.p: DeepSeek's GRPO method has the model answer the same question several times, then rewards the attempts that beat the group's average and discourages the rest.

visual.caption: Four tries at one question, marked against each other.

steps.p: Smaller models can then be trained to copy a strong reasoning model's written-out thinking. That's called distillation — a cheap way to share the skill.

cards.statement: Reinforcement learning with checkable rewards works best where answers can be verified automatically.
cards.why: True. Maths, code with tests and puzzles give a clear right-or-wrong signal for free. Where "good" is a matter of taste, you're back to needing a judge.

cards.q: DeepSeek's GRPO decides which answers to reward by…
options: Comparing each answer with the average of several answers to the same question
Asking a person to mark each one
cards.hint: Look at the bar chart in step 4.
cards.why: Comparing within the group. Better-than-average attempts are reinforced; worse ones are discouraged. Using the group as the yardstick avoids training a separate scoring model.

cards.title: DeepSeek-R1-Zero learned to reason at length through reinforcement learning alone — without first being shown example reasoning.
cards.detail: Its 2025 paper describes the model learning to re-check and rethink its work, including an "aha moment" where it spontaneously paused to reconsider its approach.

cards.q: DeepSeek trained small models to copy R1's written-out reasoning. This is called…
cards.why: Distillation. A big "teacher" model's outputs become training examples for a small "student". The student picks up much of the skill for a fraction of the cost.

cards.q: Why is this kind of training harder to use for writing a good poem?
options: There's no automatic way to check whether a poem is "right"
Poems aren't allowed in training data
cards.hint: Look at the two columns in step 1.
cards.why: No answer key. The method relies on a reliable right-or-wrong check. For a poem there's only taste, which needs a judge — human or AI — and judges can be gamed.

cards.title: Ask the model to check its own work
cards.body: Models trained with reasoning practice are good at spotting mistakes when asked. After an answer that matters, ask it to look for errors and fix them.
cards.challenge: Next time you ask an AI a maths or logic question, follow up with: "Check that step by step — is anything wrong?"
